title: The boy in the temple (Luke 2:41–52)
hookLine: twelve-year-old Jesus goes missing for three days and is found asking questions
tomorrow: The wild man by the river

cards: A crowded store. A parent turns around, and the child isn't there. Now stretch that moment to three days.

Every year, Luke says, Mary and Joseph go up to Jerusalem for Passover, and this year Jesus is twelve. When the feast ends they start home with a big group of relatives and neighbors, assuming he's somewhere in the crowd.
A whole day's walk later they look for him, and he's gone. They turn back. Three days of searching a packed city.

teach.b: They find him in the temple courts, "sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions." Doctors here means teachers, the scholars of the law. He isn't lecturing them.
He's listening, and asking, and everyone who hears him is astonished at his understanding and his answers.
Then Mary speaks, in the voice of a frightened parent: "Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."
The boy's answer is the first thing Jesus says in Luke's Gospel: "How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"
A small puzzle: the Greek is short and can be read two ways, my Father's business or my Father's house. Translators still choose between them. Either way, his first words point to God as his Father.
And his parents, Luke says plainly, didn't understand.
He goes home with them and is obedient to them, and Mary, again, keeps all these sayings in her heart. The four Gospels tell no other story from the years between his infancy and his adult life.
Years of silence, and the one scene we're given is a boy asking questions in the house of God.

teach.h: NO OTHER STORY FROM THOSE YEARS.
teach.b: Then one line for everything after: "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man."

teach.h: JESUS INCREASED IN WISDOM AND STATURE.
teach.b: Even he grew, a little at a time.

how: Many churches read this story in the Christmas season, and Catholics pray it as the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary, the finding in the temple. Christian art often shows the boy seated among the teachers.

games.q: you're Mary. after three days you find your son among the teachers in the temple. what do you say?
o: nothing. just hug him and leave.
son, why have you done this to us? we searched for you, sorrowing.
scold him in front of everyone.
games.why: Mary asks why, and says his father and she sought him sorrowing. his answer, about his Father's business, is the first thing Jesus says in Luke.

practice: Look for a question you've been carrying, about God, about your life, about something you were taught that never quite made sense: a real one, not a polite one.

Some people hide their questions because they think faith means having answers, but the boy in this story sits in the temple asking, so say yours to yourself plainly, in one sentence. If you pray, bring it to God just as it is.

wordCard.voice: Doctors. The King James word for the temple scholars, the teachers of the law that twelve-year-old Jesus sat among, listening and asking questions.

orig.note: Greek: teacher. Luke finds the boy in the midst of the teachers; later, people will call him teacher too.

carryVoice: Your line: questions belong in the temple. Tomorrow, a wild man by the river, and the grown-up years begin. That's day forty-six.
